utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and our new colleague, Aleksandar Aleksic, legal consultant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If there are no housekeeping or other preliminary matters -- yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just one if I may, and it is with regards to the next witness. Yesterday we received a joint response from the Defence with regard to the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list to add three documents for the purposes of ST-023's testimony. Since this witness may testify as soon as this Friday, we ask that we just give a brief reply here today with regard to one of the issues that the Defence raised in their response, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You propose to do that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it will take literally two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Can I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And this is with regard to paragraph 5 of the joint response, where the Defence argue that there's no need to add these three documents to the Prosecution's exhibit list because the witness can provide oral testimony with regard to the matters covered by those documents. These particular documents are payroll records and, as this Trial Chamber has seen, with other witnesses and other payroll records they are quite extensive in the number of names and other information contained upon them. As a time-saving measure, the Prosecution has taken the approach that rather than going through every single name on a payroll list that the witness simply confirms that the list is accurate with regard to that organisation or unit. Otherwise, it would require the Prosecution to go name by name and that probably wouldn't serve any purpose. Secondly, at this stage, the Prosecution doesn't know whether the Defence challenges the evidence contained within these documents, and, of course, these documents are corroborative of the evidence of the witness and, therefore, it does serve a purpose beyond the witness's oral testimony. Now, of course, the witness is going to be proofed. He hasn't been shown these documents. He will be shown them during proofing and if he is able to authentic them or verify them, then, of course, we would proceed with showing him during his testimony for that limited purpose. And with that, the Prosecution, again, requests that the Trial Chamber grant its motion to add these three documents to its exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, there is a matter before the witness is brought in to court. I sent yesterday afternoon around 5.00 p.m. an information by mail to legal officers and my friends from the Prosecutor's office, informing the parties that the -- the Stanisic Defence will seek to add additional time to cross-examination of this witness. And I don't know if Your Honours would like to hear me now on that, or after the witness finishes his direct. Also in that -- in that mail, I -- I informed Trial Chamber that I'm afraid that due to these circumstances, I will not be able to -- to argue the exhumations on Thursday but on Friday only as originally estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We've seen the -- your note, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, could you remind me as to how much additional time you had -- I know it's a total of four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I made a mistake. For some reason I thought that we had now estimated two hours but we estimated three hours, so I'm asking for an additional hour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To deal with these additional documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Granted as prayed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Olmsted, are you ready to have the usher escort your witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're ready for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Again, good morning, sir. I trust you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I trust with you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony today. I will begin by asking you to read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. May I begin, first of all, sir, to ask you to state your name and your date of birth and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Gojko Vasic. I was born on the 13th of March, 1958, at Gornja Podgora, in the municipality of Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what's your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I ask you what was your occupation in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since 1986 I have been with the police, which means that in 1992, also, I worked as a crime police investigator at the SJB of Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, have you ever testified before this Tribunal in any of the cases that are -- have been tried here in this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Or have you testified at home in any of the domestic courts on matters related to the conflict in -- in the former Balkan region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well then. Let me then explain to you how the proceedings unfold before this Court. You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution, and I take it that you have already met with the Prosecutor, who is sitting to your right, Mr. Olmsted. He will begin by examining you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- in-chief, and the Prosecution has been granted two hours to complete its examination-in-chief. You are being called under a specific rule in our Rules of Procedure, according to which we seek to expedite the testimony by asking you to confirm that the statements you have previously given to the Prosecution are correct and that you would be willing to give the same answers if you were put the same questions again today. That's the way in which we seek to have these statements tendered into evidence more quickly than we would be able to do if we were to go through them page by page. So if there is any deviance or anything you have to add or to correct in the statements, then make sure that you provide this information to the Court here today. When the Prosecution has completed its examination-in-chief, the counsels for the Defence, Mr. Zecevic for Mr. Mico Stanisic and Counsel Krgovic for the accused Stojan Zupljanin will then begin their cross-examination. Counsel for Mr. Stanisic has asked for three hours for his cross-examination, and counsel for Mr. Zupljanin has asked for one hour. And after that, again, the Prosecution will have the possibility to have a re-direct examination of you in order to finalise some of the questions that were raised in cross-examination. So this will take us through the entire hearing today and probably also tomorrow. At any point the Judges may also put question to you, if there is anything that we need to have clarified as part of your testimony. We normally run the hearings at sessions lasting approximately one hour and a half after which the tapings need to be changed. Everything that goes on here in the courtroom is recorded but the tapes need to be changed, and so every 90 minutes we will have a 20-minute break. And we will have to adjourn this morning's hearings at 1.45 this afternoon, and then we will resume tomorrow again at 9.00 and run until 1.45. If at any point you wish to have a break or you need to rest, then please do not hesitate to indicate this to us and we will comply with your requests immediately. Is there any questions you would like to put to the Chamber before we begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Then the only thing I have to do is to remind you that you have given the solemn declaration and that you are therefore required to tell the truth and I should remind that you there is a severe penalty for providing a false or incomplete testimony before this Tribunal. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and just to clarify, my examination will be much closer to half an hour rather than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to testifying today, did you have an opportunity to review your written statements from 25 June 2009, 1 April 2010, and 30 July 2010?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And with regard to the 1 April 2010 statement, did you have some revisions to some of the annexes to that statement, as well as one additional annex?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: The revisions were about some things that weren't precise enough at the outset, such as the log-book of crimes and also regarding the events that were entered from April till December 1992, but those were events that happened earlier; only they were entered later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen 65 ter 10406.1 and I ask that this not be published, the reason being as -- at least the first annex mentions some victims of rape crimes, and I wouldn't want that to get beyond this Chamber. And the number again is 10406.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see in the bottom right-hand corner -- we can just have the B/C/S up for now. We will put the English up in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But anyway, for purposes for right now, there is -- there are English translations of these revised annexes and they have been loaded into e-court this morning, but we'll get them on the screen. But for purposes right now, we don't need to have the English ones necessarily in front of us. What I want the witness to do is -- if he could confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the lower right-hand corner it contains your initials and the date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why don't we just quickly flip through these pages and just -- if can you confirm after you have seen them that these are the revisions and the added annex that you made during proofing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could just flip through to page 3. And page 4.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And page 6.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Page 7.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, page 8.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I first want to talk about, actually, this last annex that we're looking at right now. Which annex did you add to your statement?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Knezevo annex or annex 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And is that a result of your review of the Knezevo police crime register after you completed your April 2010 statement?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Knezevo was added yesterday, and Kotor Varos was changed earlier, in relation to the number of crimes from April to December and because we have determined that one criminal register or crime register was logged in Kotor Varos actually wasn't devoted to crimes but to work of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you've already stated that the revisions to the various annexes were primarily to clarify any ambiguities that existed within the annexes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do these revisions substantially change or alter your statistical findings?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Not in their essence. These are just corrections of a minor importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: With these changes to the annex as well as this additional annex for Knezevo, are you satisfied that the information contained in your three statements is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the limited the time I have, I wasn't planning on going through each of the revisions to these various annexes as the witness has stated they are minor. They are there to eliminate ambiguities and just to make sure that they're very clear. I will just note that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, Could you tell us what your current position is with RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I am -- I'm in vein here. We received yesterday the revised chart done by this chance. Now, for the first time I understand that one municipality has been added, and I'm -- I'm in no position at this point to identify what are the changes made to the previous. Because the -- the original annex has 17 subannexes. This one, the revised annex, I believe has seven. One municipality has been added, which does not appear on the original annexes; that is the municipality of Knezevo, and the -- the six -- the six -- the six municipalities have been revised. I am -- I'm not in a position, at this point, or was able yesterday during the night to identify what are the changes. So, respectively I would ask the Trial Chamber to grant the time to Mr. Olmsted so he can explain us what are the changes and how the changes appeared during the proofing of the witness yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, is there a more efficient way of addressing Mr. Zecevic's legitimate concerns -- [microphone not activated] that he has proposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We will propose to admit with his 92 ter package the original annexes as well as the revised one and that will allow the Trial Chamber, the Defence, to compare them themselves and see what the changes are. This witness has said that they're minor. They don't have a major impact on his findings, and I think if we went through them one by one it would take a bit of time to do that. I certainly can do that. I'm not sure we'll get any further with that and, of course, the Defence have opportunity during cross-examination to go over any of the revisions with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I take your point, Mr. Olmsted, about the changes being minor. Of course, that's a matter of perception, and Mr. Zecevic, where he would have had an opportunity to compare and contrast himself, may agree with you or he may disagree with you. I'm only wondering whether as a purely practical matter his - and I repeat what I said earlier - his legitimate concern can be addressed. And, Mr. Zecevic, rather than Mr. Olmsted, as you propose, taking the time to go through it, I'm wondering whether the more efficient course might not be for the Chamber to take a slightly extended break between sessions so that either before you begin your cross-examination or during your cross-examination, you have the -- you're in a position to familiarize yourself with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is acceptable for us, that we receive a sort of a longer break before our start of cross-examination and I will be able to identify that. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, could you tell what us what your current position with RS MUP is.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: I am currently the head or director of police of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us very briefly what your primary responsibilities are in that position.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Director of police of Republika Srpska is a senior officer of the operative segment in the Ministry of Interior. He is in command of the uniformed police and is in charge of implementing the law in the territory of Republika Srpska and the legality of the work of the police as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who is your immediate superior or supervisor?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior is the minister of the interior. And I was appointed to the position that I'm at by the government of the Republika Srpska. So my responsibility is to the minister and the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what position did you hold prior to your current position, the position you held when you were primarily engaged in performing the analysis we're going to be talking about today.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: For the four or five years before that, I was head of the administration of criminal police. In other words, I was the senior officer of the crime or criminal police of Republika Srpska. Before that, I was the chief of sector of criminal police in CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned during Judge Harhoff's questions in 1992 that you were a crime Inspector at SJB Laktasi. Can you tell us where Laktasi is?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Station of Laktasi or the municipality of Laktasi is north of Banja Luka. It's an area with about 30.000 inhabitants, predominantly of Serbian ethnicity. That was the situation before the war as well. The station before the war had about 30 employees. Some of them were police members and others were administrative staff. I don't know whether I've given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. Now you're aware that the indictment in this case pertains to 20 municipalities. As a crime inspector in Laktasi in 1992, how much contact did you personally have with those 20 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, I worked exclusively in the area of the municipality of Laktasi, and my contacts with other municipalities happened very seldom. It's the territorial jurisdiction that's important in our work, and police works in their own respective areas. We had the most contacts, of course, with the neighbouring municipalities such as Banja Luka, Gradiska, Srbac, Prnjavor, Celinac, and our contacts mainly boiled down to cases where criminal groups would be arrested that had committed crimes in multiple municipalities, then we would work together on that. We had best cooperation both before the war and during and after the war with the Banja Luka police station or the centre, depending on the gravity of the crime we were working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, do you have any personal knowledge from 1992 of the circumstances surrounding any of the criminal reports that are included in your statistical analysis of the crime registers?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: No. Bearing in mind that all these crimes were crimes committed in other areas. I could have only known about them indirectly, either from the media, although the media, at the time, also, had problems. There were current power failures there, so to be precise, it was very difficult to transfer informations, so even those information that was necessary for the police work. To put it simply, information traffic was not functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The scope of your project is described in your written statements. But just to summarize briefly, you were requested to really perform two tasks: First, to identify entries in the 1992 police crime registers relating to crimes listed in the schedules to the indictment in this case; and, secondly, to identify entries in the 1992 registers for serious crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims? Can you tell us, what kinds of serious crimes did you look for in these registers?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: My first task was to identify the registers, or log-books, that were kept in various stations because in transfer, the recording was made of the criminal register book of the on-site investigation book and so on. And sometimes one could even find other support documents for the work. And in relation to the number of crimes that were logged in, and this number is very high, we have analysed only those that are related to the indictments -- in other words, events that took place in 1992 are uncovered by the indictment. What can be found in this -- in these registers is, first of all, number of crimes that were logged in each record book, or the number of them in the period between April and December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we're going to into a little more detail about the registers in a second. But I want to ask you this question. You were also trying to identify serious crimes, and I just want you to explain to the Trial Chamber what kinds of serious crimes you were looking for.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: I was asked to identify murders, attempted murders, rape, causing of general danger, war crimes, and these crimes -- these are crimes for which it was necessary first to determine those that were committed under the non-Serb population by the police members. Secondly, serious crimes against non-Serbs committed by Serbian perpetrators. Then crimes against non-Serbs by an unknown perpetrators. And then there was a group of those where it could not be determined, as it's stated in the register, whether the victim was a Serb or a non-Serb. And the last column is about those crimes where Serbs were the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, with regard to serious crimes, you were looking for -- just looking at the description of the crimes, you were looking for crimes of violence, essentially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Although when one speaks about crimes of violence or crimes that involve elements of hostile or enemy activity, in 1992 there was a law in effect in both Republika Srpska and Federation. The Federation whereby certain acts were not qualified as crimes but could have had significant effects on relations between nations, such as destroying somebody's property or entering somebody's home, or causing bodily grievance which were crimes where people normally would have had to file a report and deal with them through courts themselves. These crimes were not encompassed by this. Violent crimes only include causing general dangers, rapes, murders, and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, your statements and annexes do not include the municipalities of Ilijas, Vogosca, Kljuc or Donji Vakuf. Do you know what happened to the 1992 crime registers from those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware what may have happened with those registers, although the people who worked in the department for war crimes have tried to locate the documents. However, they failed in their attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your statements, you describe the various log-books and registers maintained by the police in 1992 and the procedures for recording that information -- recording various information into those books. Since your statistical analysis focused on the crime registers or the KUs, or K-Us, I want to ask you a few questions regarding the crime registers. Can you tell us what was the purpose of the police crime registers?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: In every municipality, there was kept one criminal register where one would log all crimes -- or, rather, or all reported crimes by a known or unknown perpetrator that were then passed on to the relevant prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned unknown perpetrator criminal reports. Can you tell us, once the police identified a perpetrator who was previously unknown, was this information reflected in the criminal register, the crime register?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: If a perpetrator of a crime is determined, a crime that was earlier reported as committed by unknown perpetrator, then a report would be sent to the prosecutor who was dealing with the case. And then in the same column where it is required, it would said who the perpetrator was. And in that way, this is cleared from the register for unknown perpetrators and moved to the -- to the -- to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, once the perpetrator is identified, the police would go back to the original entry for that criminal report and record the name of the perpetrator they were able to identify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. In that column, it would -- one would see NN, unknown perpetrator, and once a perpetrator was identified, one would list -- if there were more of them, at least one of them. Sometimes there would be enough room to put in all the perpetrators although there were crimes that involved more than 20 of them; whereas, the boxes include enough space for, let's say, four of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, most of what you have elicited from the witness is amply explained in his three statements, and you are running close to the half-hour that you had asked for. And I take this opportunity also to correct myself. I was erroneously under the impression that you had been given two hours, but, in fact, you have only been given 30 minutes and they are just about to expire, so please round up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I did want to highlight a couple of things. I know that the practice is not to do so with 92 ter witnesses, so I'm going to move on. I do want to show one example of one of these annexes so that Your Honours have a good understanding of it. Let me ask one last question, though, about what this witness did to undertake this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Besides the log-books, themselves, Mr. Vasic, did you use any other resources to identify criminal reports that fell within the scope of this project?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to the log-books or crime registers, I looked into book of on-sites -- books of on-site investigation -- or, rather, for one municipality, at least for the municipality of Trebinje I did that, to see -- to compare whether there were crimes and on-site investigations that matched. And in such a way, I cleared things up. I also looked at supporting log-books. And in some municipalities, such as Brcko, one could not find a standard log-book. Instead, they kept just a support type of log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And beyond the physical books themselves, did you use other resources to assist you in making sure you're identifying the criminal reports accurately? Did you use other resources available to you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the position that I was holding at the time, I asked the stations that are encompassed by the indictment to prepare analysis for the period, and then I compared the data we found with their analysis, in order to remove any possible mistakes or unclear issues. For instance, the recording of log-books I had was not legible properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at the exhibit that's in front of us. It's 65 ter 10406.1. If we can turn to the first page. And this is, when we get there, it will be the revised annex you prepared for Kotor Varos. And let me just lay some foundation here. We see -- there's three columns. The first column is the statistical question that was presented to you and you describe those for us. The second contains the total number of criminal reports that you were able to identify in response to each of those questions. And the third column contains the entry numbers in the criminal register for each of those reports. Now, the table for Kotor Varos -- the table for Kotor Varos is a bit different because we see that some of the entry numbers in the third column have question marks next to them. Can you explain to us what the question marks mean?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: The first time we reviewed the documentation concerning Kotor Varos in the standardized form of the crime register, there were 350 crimes registered, I believe. But nobody noticed then that it concerned ancillary documents rather than the crime register. All the rubrics were filled in just the same as you do in the crime register, but it was, in fact, supporting documentation where many of these cases were archived in Kotor Varos. Thus, for instance, there is an item in the second line, the crime of rape, one case with two victims, under item 77 of that register, and it was not prosecuted and it involves a member of the special detachment. From this documentation, it was impossible to establish whether the number of crimes was not higher because some cases were referred to the military prosecutor, in view of the fact that, at that time, there were certain military operations in Kotor Varos and the military command had jurisdiction, and the military police and the military prosecutor were able to deal with that. However, you cannot see that from the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify. For the purposes of this annex, you in fact reviewed two log-books. First, the open cases log-book, which is maintained by the crime investigation team; and secondly, you reviewed the crime register, the KU for Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the crime register, out of these 350-something crimes, 84 are logged in. However, 38 crimes belong in the period from April through December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for the entries you identified in the open case log-book, were you able to find those, the ones you have designated with a question mark, in the crime register?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: No. That's why the question mark was put there. Because these are serious crimes that were logged in this ancillary documentation but do not feature in this official register. For instance, in that log-book, we couldn't even find the murder of Stevan Markovic and one Stevilovic who were killed in Kotor Varos sometime in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to look at this entry 277, the double rape case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to item 6 where there is one war crime against Serb victims identified. And if we may have on the screen now 65 ter 10409. And I ask this not be published because we will be seeing names of victims. And if we can turn to page 108 of the B/C/S, page 4 of the English. And while they're doing that, I'll just point out for the record that the ERN numbers for the pages we're looking at do not correspond with the ERN range put in his statement, and the reason being that is they're the same log-book but they were a different quality of photographs of them taken, and so we're showing him now the better quality one, but essentially it's -- it is in fact the same log-book. And if we can zoom in on entry 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, we see that it shows that one of the victims reported her and another woman's rape by Danko Kajkut. And I think you mentioned at the time that Danko Kajkut was with the special detachment. If we look at column 10 is that what is in fact reported in this book, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can scroll over in the B/C/S to column 19. And we have to turn the page in the English to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see under column 19 there's handwritten A/A. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: That means the case was filed in the archives as far as further checks are concerned in the public security station of Kotor Varos, and we have the initials of the man who conducted the previous checks; that is, investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If a criminal report was filed for a case in this open cases log-book, would that be reflected in the entry for that case?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: One would see in the crime register a new number and a new entry on the condition that the public security station had finalized the investigation and submitted the criminal report to the prosecutor's office. But if the criminal case had been referred to the military authorities, which we can't see from this, then it would appear as archived in the register. This just means, as far as the public security station is concerned, that no further work is being done. Just looking at a specific case in this book, you cannot see whether and why a case has been archived. It could have been archived, hypothetically speaking, because the perpetrator was found dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if this -- the last part of the witness's answer was not recorded as I heard it. So maybe you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could just clarify the last part of your testimony with regard to what it meant that the case was archived. You mentioned this does not indicate what -- why it was archived. Can you just make clear what -- what your point was on that issue.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: From this record, you cannot see why a case has been archived. In other words, what the reason was to stop further work on this case. That could have been because the military security had taken it over, or because a report has been attached that the perpetrator is dead or out of reach, in which case an AP bulletin would have been issued. Those could have been the reasons. Another reason could have been that there are no elements of crime. For instance, if a rape was reported in a time-period when it's impossible to prove it, and that is to say if several days have elapsed. In other words, if it was impossible to find physical evidence apart from finding a number of witnesses who could also confirm the -- the words of the injured party, in a case of rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 106 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Olmsted, that would be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to show the related log-book to this, and then I will be completed with my questions if that is at all possible. Just to show the link between the two books. I think I have five minutes left, maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see here under entry 58 -- I'm sorry, entry 259 and Article 124, armed rebellion case against a number of individuals. If we scroll over to column 24 in the B/C/S, we see in column 24 written 58/92. Is that a cross-reference to the criminal register for Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen 65 ter 10408. This is the Kotor Varos crime register for 1992. And if we could turn to page 9 of the B/C/S, page 6 of the English. And if we can zoom in under -- well, zoom in on entry 58. Scroll over a bit to the -- to the left-hand side. The other way. No, other way and bring up page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see here entry 58 that a criminal report was filed against a number of individuals for armed rebellion. So this is the entry that was referenced in the open case log-book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 11 of the B/C/S; page 8 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see entry 71 is a criminal report submitted by CSB Banja Luka for war crimes committed against 16 Serbs from Serdar. Is this the war crime case against Serb victims that you identified in the annex to Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see in column 7 that at the top of the entry it indicates that the perpetrators are unknown. It says NN. But then we see in different handwriting below it, in handwriting the name Marko Sipura. Is this an example where the perpetrator is later identified by the police and then they insert that perpetrator's name into the entry?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Precisely. The period that elapsed from the first report of the crime and the identification of the perpetrator was probably longer than was necessary to report a crime involving an unidentified perpetrator. Because, in those circumstances, it was quite difficult to identify the perpetrator and find the evidence. There must have been quite a while before the first report of the crime and the identification of the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what ethnicity Marko Sipura has?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: I believe he is a Croat. There were 13 other perpetrators involved, and from the moment when this war crime was committed until they were identified, there must have been quite a while. And in this case, perhaps three or four perpetrators were known from the start but we needed to identify the others, and the victim who survived this massacre was probably of some help in the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can scroll over in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see -- oh, that's too far. Back a little bit. And we can zoom in on column 13. We see that this case was submitted to the military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if the police investigate a case and they determine that it falls within the military jurisdiction, that case is recorded in this book as well?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: On the condition that the police has completed the entire investigation and collection of evidence. However, if, from the start, the police is aware that a case could fall within the jurisdiction of the military authorities, then they are reported to the military security, and then a decision is made that the military security should probably take that case over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic, could you just clarify this last point with us, because I think I saw in column 12 that the crime which is the subject of these headings was characterised as a war crime against civilians. So my question to you is: Under which circumstances would a criminal case, such as the one we have in front of us, be referred under the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All cases involving crimes committed by military or paramilitary units are referred to the military authorities, regardless of whether they were non-Serbs or acting in non-Serb territory, or otherwise. All crimes perpetrated by organised military formations are referred to the military prosecutor. These persons involved here were military conscripts, and even if they had not responded to mobilisation call-up, they would still fall within the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor. If they were responsible for an armed insurgency in that territory, they would still fall within the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor, regardless of the fact that the injured parties were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the perpetrators in this case, I understand, were of Croat ethnicity. Were they under the command of the -- of the army? So were they regarded as members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. They were members of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, or members of -- if you want to put it this way, non-Serb military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So they were regarded as members of the armed forces of the enemy in this conflict at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But you also mentioned paramilitary groups. That's what came out in your testimony in translation in any case. How would paramilitary, Serb paramilitary formations be characterised? Would they fall under the jurisdiction of -- and -- and the command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they had committed a crime, they would fall under the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor and the military security organs, because men over the age of 18 who had done their military service were duty-bound to report to their units, rather than setting up independent groups and moving about, especially not carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic -- sorry, Mr. Zecevic, we're so near the time for the break that we would rise now. Is it your preference that we take this extended break now or would you prefer -- or is it more convenient to resume at the regular time and you take the witness as far as you could and then take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in order to have the continuity, I would prefer the break, if it can be this break that is extended, Your Honours. That would be my preference. There is just one question I would need to clarify with my learned friend from the Prosecutor's side, because I'm not -- at this point, I'm not really clear what is the 92 ter package for this witness. Does the 92 ter package consist of 10406 and 10406.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case. What the -- what 10406.1 is are the -- basically revisions, corrections and additions to his 1 April 2010 annexes. So to the extent that they're not covered by the revisions, then you will resort to the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand now. Your Honours, I would need probably additional 15 to 20 minutes to the -- to the original time of the break, if that can be given to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So should we think in terms of resuming at 11.00 or 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 11.00 is perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: All right. 11.00 it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted or Mr. Hannis, while we're waiting for the witness we have two small questions in regard to the viva voce estimates of the witnesses you -- you propose to be 92 bis in the 44 extra witnesses for adjudicated facts. You with me? So two question. This there is one -- Witness ST-232 is listed on the estimate -- the estimate list you gave us last week as being changed from Rule 92 bis to 92 quater witness. Could you indicate us what the reason of this change is. If not immediately ... And the second question is, ST-240. Is listed with a viva voce estimate of 0 hours. I suppose that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I think I can address both the -- answer both those questions for you after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have to ask you something, because we heard that this is the first time you're testifying before this Tribunal. Because of the interpretation, we must make a pause and speak slower for the interpreters to have enough time to interpret everything and for it to be recorded in the transcript. Because if you answer too soon, then we may overlap and it will not -- it won't be possible for the interpreters to interpret.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you're an employee of the Ministry of Interior and you have been employed there for 25 years; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Currently, if I understood correctly, you're the director of the police in the RS, right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the OTP asked you to draft the report that you drafted, due to your knowledge of the subject matter and due to your long experience in -- with these things, right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: The first reason why I was supposed to assist the OTP was to identify the log-books and registers for it to be known what the log-book of events was, what the criminal register was, and what some possible ancillary documents were. Before the war, during the war, and after the war I have been with the crime police, and we reached agreement within the ministry for me to be the OTP's witness in this trial. Later on, requests were also made regarding the analyses of serious crimes; also upon the request of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the Prosecution gave you the six questions. That can be found in your schematics that you made. And you dealt with them municipality by municipality and consulting various documents in the process; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, it's a fact, isn't it, that, based on consulting exclusively the criminal register, the KU register, it isn't possible to ascertain with perfect certainty all these facts. It is the position of the Defence that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we request that -- when the Defence asks questions they don't state, This is the position of the Defence. They just ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm a bit confused. So far I have been reminded on numerous occasions that the -- that the -- the Defence is supposed to apply the Rule 90(H)(ii), where I have to state our case to the witness. Now, when I'm trying to do that, I get the objection from the Prosecution. I would like that the Prosecution clarifies its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is, yes, the Defence do have to state their position but they don't have to phrase the question in a way saying that, This is what we, as a Defence, are contending with a witness. It's just put the question to the witness and have him answer it, without any clause in there saying, This is the position we're taking on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's a question of how the question is phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I put it to you that a comprehensive image based on the questions put to you by the Prosecution can be depicted only after reviewing all the KU registers, log-books of daily events, and the register of on-site investigation -- investigations, which was kept with each individual SJB or CSB respectively. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: A complete image of everything that was happening can be painted this way, but an analysis of the log-book of daily events, the KU register, and the other register would include about 50.000 entries, which is a task much too demanding for an individual to carry out, especially considering that I have to go about my regular business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your reply correctly, you agree with my statement that to get a complete picture of the events and provide answers to these questions, it would be necessary, as far as the police is concerned, to consult three documents: The KU register, the log-book of daily events, and the register of on-site investigations. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is how you check things when auditing a police station. You check whether all events were investigated. If so, whether on-site investigations were made, and whether reports were filed with the prosecutor's office. That would be a comprehensive analysis which one person cannot make himself, especially not in such a short period that. Would require a team of analysts. The questions put to me -- or, rather, the requests made, did not include all this because it would have been clear that I wouldn't be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the information contained in your schematics and snap-shots of the situation basically is problem-ridden. Namely, it is possible that the information is not complete or that your analysis was not accompanied by an analysis of other documents.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I can answer either in the affirmative or the -- in the negative. The question is what was entered in the KU register. So the scope of my work was clearly de-limited by the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what I listed -- I mean, the log-books and registers kept at SJBs, in accordance with the rules of service and at the CSBs; in other words, in the bodies of the Ministry of Interior, are not enough. The registers of the public prosecutor's office and the court would also have to be consulted to get a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: The log-books and registers of the public prosecutor's office and the courts are also necessary to get a complete picture of what not only the police but also the citizens filed with these bodies reported to them. In accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina then, stipulated that reports could be filed with the public prosecutor's office either orally or in writing. So the place where you could get a complete picture of what was reported to the police and the public prosecutor's office is the log-book of daily events, plus the log-book of the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the direct reporting of crimes, let me explain a bit or ... Let's assume that an injured party after a crime has been committed by which he or she has been injured, in accordance with the rules and regulations in force then, they could file a criminal report directly with the public prosecutor's office in writing or orally, by which the police would have been excluded from the process, because the police wouldn't know that such a criminal report was received by the public prosecutor's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the first phase. The public prosecutor's office, if they can complete the investigation themselves, they can do so. But most often, the public prosecutor's office will send a request to the SJB in charge to verify or to conduct a verification on the ground. And no matter whether this document was received from the public prosecutor's office, it will be recorded in the KU register.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain the Trial Chamber and everybody present how things are done, so let us focus and proceed in a chronological sequence. So the injured party had the right to file a criminal report directly with the public prosecutor's office in writing or orally. Your answer was affirmative, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, it was customary for the public prosecutor to forward this report to the police with some instructions or requests to collect information to establish facts and the like; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, after those instructions of the prosecutor to collect information or establish facts were carried out, the police would submit that information to the prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, can you tell us - and I'm now returning to the log-book of daily events - were all events entered in that log-book about which the officer on duty learned during that day?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. All events would be entered in the log-book of daily events without any censoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the ratio was between the number of entries and the crimes that are included in that log-book of daily events? The rough ratio, in accordance with your experience.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Well, it should be 1:5 -- from 1:5 to 1:10. More likely toward 1:10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, that would mean in the log-book of daily incidents kept by a certain public security station one would find, let's say, ten information -- items of information about certain events taking place on a certain day, and one of those would be about a crime -- a crime that was committed on that day.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr. Vasic, even before the unfortunate events, you had worked in the Ministry of the Interior, and it is a fact, isn't it, that with the start of the war, first in former Yugoslavia in general and in Bosnia and Herzegovina in particular, there was a huge increase in the number of crimes of -- or behaviour of criminal nature, in relation to the period before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that certain types of especially serious crimes in the period before the war was rather seldom occurring in the territory of former Yugoslavia. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Crimes of murder, of causing general danger, and even certain crimes of -- of robbery were of a much lower frequency than in the war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The trends in the former Yugoslavia were on the decrease before the war, when we're talking about such crimes.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The number of murders was, all the time, decreasing, and crimes involving causing general danger was almost non- existence because weapons were not widespread. All the weapons were either in the barracks or with the army, and rifles that were used for hunting and such were not very often used in such a -- types of crimes, and especially explosives were an exception to the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the situation we have just described, it is a fact that public security stations on the territory of former Yugoslavia, SFRY, were not really well-equipped, especially in terms of forensic equipment, to conduct good quality investigation of serious crimes. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Well, that is natural. Certain types of crimes, police never received reports about them, so there was no reason for the police to invest so much into working on that type of crimes [as interpreted]. Issues like that simply require a lot of funds, and before the war, with all the funds invested, you wouldn't have seen that much of an improvement. However, in 1992, of course, having had that -- those equipment would have helped a lot, because investigations would have proceeded with more expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Essentially, in time when the war broke out, and when the number of extremely serious crimes increased, the police, having at their disposal what they had in former Yugoslavia, was not sufficiently equipped to investigate such serious crimes. Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to raise an objection here. It seems like my learned friend is asking questions regarding what is happening throughout the Republika Srpska or the former Yugoslavia while this witness has clearly stated that he was a crime inspector in one municipality and I think we're -- we lack foundation here for him to be answering questions about what was happening in 1992 outside of Laktasi. If that -- if my learned friend's questions are directed at Laktasi I think that's fair. But if he's talking beyond his municipality, I think there needs to be some more foundation laid here as to how this witness would have personal knowledge as to what was going on in other municipalities in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree with Mr. Olmsted. I was speaking in general terms intentionally, believing that it's general knowledge. But I would like to ask you, sir, to, in your answers, specify that you're talking about your public security station. So can we say that the situation was as described in your public security station where you worked?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the area of Laktasi, there were very few crimes of causing general danger, and after the breakout of the war, the number reached 100. It made up for 22 per cent of the crime in general. Only 5 or 6 per cent were properly investigated and completed, because conditions weren't existent. In some cases we didn't have equipment that would enable us to determine whether a burst of machine-gun fire against, let's say, a church in Zvornik was done from a distance of 100, 300, or 500 metres, and also because there were weapons everywhere, one could find shells all over the place, and it was very difficult to connect this with a specific crime. So for objective reasons it was impossible to determine certain things. Also, there were some cases of murder where we would have been greatly assisted had we had better forensic equipment. We didn't have DNA method capabilities. But in the area of Laktasi, we did manage to resolve all the issues involving murder cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us get back to the documents now. The documents, or at least one of the documents kept in the public security stations, was the log-book or register of on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This log-book of onsite investigations included data and information about all events and on-site investigations carried out by the public security station in its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From this log-book of on-site investigations, one can see where the investigation was carried out, based on which criminal report, and who was present at the scene.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The book is kept in chronological order. After any of the on-site investigations, information would be logged about who took part in the investigation; namely, the investigative judge, prosecutor, forensic experts, and inspector -- police inspector. Sometimes the judge or the prosecutor would authorise the investigator, the inspector to represent them, so only they would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in cases when the prosecutor or the investigative judge is present at the on-site investigation, from that moment, he or she is the person giving instructions to the police as to what to do in the following period.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They conduct the investigation, they write a report about it, and instructs the members of the team as to what to do on the site of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The situation was the same when the -- either investigative judge or the prosecutor authorises the police inspector to carry out this on-site investigation on their own. After the on-site investigation, the police inspector submits the report or the minutes to the prosecutor, who then give instructions to the police as to what to do from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Very seldom it would be only this record of the on-site investigation that would be submitted to the prosecutor and investigative judge. But in any case, then the request would be made from the police -- to the police to find out who the perpetrators were, to find out all the evidence, and from that moment on, the process would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In cases when it is clear from the on-site investigation that the perpetrator is unknown, we can take as an example one of those cases of causing general danger, or maybe a grievous bodily harm was caused, then a report is immediately made to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every on-site investigation is made in four copies: One goes to the prosecutor; one to the investigative judge; one copy is kept in the public station; and one is kept with the operative who is working on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact - and I think you spoke about it briefly during the direct examination - that, in addition to crimes that were prosecuted ex officio, there was a certain number of crimes that weren't done in such a way, that were done on the basis of a private civil [as interpreted] action.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I emphasised --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Just to make it clear, what I said was a private criminal report or criminal lawsuit. It's on page 39:25. Maybe the term itself is not clear enough so I would like to ask you to briefly explain what is this private criminal lawsuit or report.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: According to the law at the time, the Law on Criminal Proceedings of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were certain types of crimes that were to be dealt with or prosecuted ex officio, and I won't go into that, and there were also certain crimes that had to be prosecuted on the basis of private criminal lawsuit such as violation of private property or place of habitation, then threats, insults, and cases of inflammatory national hatred attempts. Because when a person comes to a police station, this is all that the police can do, report it, and we all know how such activities can -- what effect can it have on citizens that are part of, let's say, a minority group in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe this may be something that would be good to illustrate, so I'll show you a few documents that are relevant for this oral criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D00-1984 on the screen. It is tab 84; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This memo, I think the date of it is 3rd of September, 1992. CS -- can you see this, can you read it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it saying public security station Banja Luka, crime prevention and detection department. This is an accompanying memo that went with an oral criminal report a police station received in cases of theft; for instance, you would get such a report where it is not necessary to do an on-site investigation. Theft of movable property or a vehicle; namely, type of theft which does not leave traces on the site where it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you page number 2 of this document. This is -- these are the minutes of taking of the criminal report. The date is 29th of August, 1992. It is a criminal report made by Adem Rajic, son of Selim. His name clearly determines that it's a person of Muslim ethnicity; am I right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Citizen Adem Rajic is submitting a criminal report on account of an instance of causing public danger because his weekend residence had been burnt down somewhere near Banja Luka. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 3 of this document, there is a form that had to be filled in as a record of receipt of such a verbal report.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is precisely the situation you described a moment ago. The injured party comes to the police, reports a crime, the type of crime that is not prosecuted ex officio?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. This one is prosecuted ex officio because it involves causing public danger, and the police has to act and does act in a case of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. However, if the crime in question is not subject to prosecution ex officio, unlike this one, then the police would direct the citizen to file a private criminal lawsuit before a competent court.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, the police would just record it in the log-book of daily events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you touched upon this in one of the previous answers. Some very unpleasant criminal offences, such as verbal injury, violation of residence, causing damage to another's property, light bodily injury, all these criminal offences that may involve ethnic motives, nationalist motives, unfortunately were prosecuted in that system on the basis of a private criminal suit, not ex officio.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And although, in this way, individuals may intimidate others by committing such crimes, they can intimidate members of another ethnic community, the police, under the prevailing legislation, is unable to file criminal reports or take any action.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: The police is not able to file a criminal report, but from what I know about what was going on in practice, the police did try to approach such individuals and issue warnings and try to deter them from further intimidating citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, what the police officers did, did not strictly fall within their job description because such offences were subject to prosecution on the basis of a private criminal suit, but the police did that for prophylactic reasons and to defuse the general tensions?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While we're still on the subject, your first-hand knowledge originates from the police station in Laktasi where you worked before the war and throughout the war, if I understood correctly?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Until mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since it is year 1992 that is relevant to this indictment, we will restrict ourselves to that period and to the police station of Laktasi. Tell me, the situation -- the security situation in the territory of the police station Laktasi and further afield in Bosnia and Herzegovina was such that the economy and the businesses came to a halt practically immediately after the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The factories stopped working because the employees were mostly military conscripts, and if, in some cases factories did continue to operate, they did so to a much reduced capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that the developments in Slovenia and later Croatia caused the businesses to lose their markets and the markets from which they obtained raw materials.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Both. Because the -- the economy was so inter-dependant that a factory was not self-sufficient. It was not possible for a factory or a business to exist without being essentially and substantially interlinked with businesses in other territories of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, another effect of that was that businesses in the industry, commerce, and in every other line, began to close down.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. 1991 was just the beginning, and it got worse as time went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it is a fact that this began already in 1991, when the conflicts began, first in Slovenia, and then in Croatia, and this slow death of the industry resulted in the loss of many jobs?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: A significant number of people were left jobless because the industries came into -- came to a halt, and in some areas, such as Banja Luka, there were major problems in electricity supply. And then imagine a company working in the area of computers or services operating with -- with power cuts as long as 36 hours, and you know very well that many parts of the city were in a complete blackout for days on end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The only production that survived for a while was agricultural production, which also supplied food to the army.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they, too, experienced problems, because power supply was reduced and because many heads of families were military conscripts and had to join the army. And you know that in a -- in a regular family, there are not that many men, usually one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that in our system we had general conscription applying to all men.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it's also a fact that if one enterprise or one factory closes down for the reasons that we've described, those employees who did not respond to the mobilize call-up were simply left jobless, right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours. I don't know -- I don't know if you would like me to maintain the usual breaks or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps we could go an additional five minutes or so and when you reach a convenient point you could so indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I don't know, but I'd ask before you leave the Bench for this break I could two minutes to answer Judge Delvoie's question and raise one other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then maybe it is appropriate that I excuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. The usher may escort the witness from the courtroom. Mr. Vasic, we would resume your testimony at about 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Judge Delvoie, your questions regarding ST-232, a change of status as proposed to make him 92 quater. Between the time we initially contact him about being a witness to deal with the adjudicated facts, unfortunately, in July, he passed away and so he's -- he is no longer available viva. With regard to ST-240, the reasons for that estimate of zero hours is set forth in a Confidential Annex attached to the motion, and without going into private session I would refer you to that. If you still have a question after reviewing that, I can address it later. The third thing was, Ms. Korner asked me to remind you of her request concerning a decision on the Prosecution's request to add a video to be used with the upcoming witness, ST-023, because she is seeing him this afternoon and may show it to him or not, depending on the ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, that decision is in process of being refined. But in terms of the -- the portion of the application dealing with the admission of the videos, it would grant that aspect. So you may prepare yourself accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for clarification -- and for clarification, it's the 65 ter numbers 3622 and 3623, two videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While we await the arrival of the witness there are two oral decisions that we have to hand down. The Chamber remains seized of Prosecution' motion of the 5th of August to change the mode of testimony of ST-136 and ST-210. The Defence jointly responded on the 19th August opposing the motion. On the 20th of August, the Prosecution sought leave to reply and filed a reply. The Trial Chamber recalls that on 20th of August the Chamber granted the motion in respect of ST-210 and also granted leave to reply. The present decision only deals with ST-136. The Prosecution seeks to change the mode of testimony of 136 from viva voce to Rule 92 ter and requests one and a half hours for the examination-in-chief. The Chamber considers that it is in the interests of the expeditious conduct of the proceedings and in accordance with the rights of the accused to hear 136, pursuant to 92 ter. However, the Prosecution has not indicated that this witness would offer evidence beyond her Rule 92 ter statements, which total over 120 pages. Considering that there is no additional viva voce issue which would warrant more than 20 to 30 minutes, the guide-lines provide for a 92 ter witness, the Prosecution has not justified its request for more time than 20 to 30 minutes. The Trial Chamber grants the Prosecution's motion to call 136 pursuant to Rule 92 ter and allows 32 minutes for examination-in-chief. Second ruling. The Chamber is seized of three motions filed on the 3rd, 4th and 20th of August.
